entities.summary: Maurice de Saxe, a prominent soldier, general, and military theorist, played a crucial role in shaping the military landscape of 18th-century Europe. Born in 1696 to Augustus II the Strong, an illegitimate son, he initially served in the Army of the Holy Roman Empire, later joining the Imperial Army and French service. De Saxe's military prowess and strategic thinking made him a key figure in the Seven Years' War and the War of the Austrian Succession. He was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the French forces in Germany in 1745 and led them to several victories against the Prussians. De Saxe's military theories, as outlined in his book 'Le Mariage de Polonais et de Allemands' (The Marriage of Poles and Germans), emphasized the importance of mobility, adaptability, and alliances. He is considered one of the most brilliant military minds of his era, and his legacy continues to influence military strategy to this day. The city of Dresden, where de Saxe spent much of his life, remains a testament to his enduring impact on European military history.
